verify.search_note: All 8 searches returned current Apple pages (no /10.7/ URLs were used as sources). Three tricks are KEEP (1, 5) or FIX (0, 2, 3, 4, 6). The biggest fixes were to the rewritten tricks. Trick 2 now uses Apple's exact dialog name, 'Replace existing sound', and drops the unsupported 'check your filter and envelope' hedge. Trick 3 dropped 'without shifting pitch', which Apple contradicts: the pitch follows the key you play.

tricks.original_title: Know the four modes and pick deliberately
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Choose a Quick Sampler mode' page confirms all four modes. Apple does not say One Shot is for 'stabs': it names drum loop playback and effects use. 'Choosing the mode is 90% of the work' is an unsupported claim dressed as fact, so it was removed. Classic was reworded to Apple's description.
tricks.final_title: Know the four modes and pick deliberately
tricks.final_body: Classic plays the sample while you hold a key, the way to play a sound across the keyboard. One Shot plays from start marker to end marker on each note, good for drum loops and effects. Slice chops a sample into slices mapped to keys. Recorder captures live input as an audio recording.

sources.label: Apple — Choose a Quick Sampler mode in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: In Classic mode the sample plays while you hold a key; it is the most useful mode for playing a sound across the keyboard range. One Shot plays from the start marker to the end marker and is great for drum loop playback and effects use. Slice divides samples into slices mapped to keys from the start key. Recorder captures any audio signal as an audio recording.

tricks.original_title: Use Slice mode with Transient detection on any break
tricks.reason: Apple's Slice mode page confirms three things. The Transient option sets slice markers from detected transients. Slices are mapped to keys. Dragging from the lower part of the waveform display to a track creates a MIDI region with a note for each slice.
tricks.final_title: Use Slice mode with Transient detection on any break
tricks.final_body: Load a drum loop, switch to Slice, and every hit is mapped to its own key. Drag from the lower waveform display into the Tracks area to get the MIDI — the original groove, fully rearrangeable.

sources.label: Apple — Quick Sampler Slice mode in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Choosing Transient from the Mode pop-up menu sets the number of slice markers from transients detected in the audio file. Clicking in the lower part of the waveform display and dragging to a software instrument/MIDI track creates a MIDI region with note-on events for each slice. The notes are placed sequentially so playback sounds like the original, and they can be edited like any MIDI region.

sources.label: Apple — Choose a Quick Sampler mode in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Slice mode divides samples into multiple segments (slices) mapped to keys starting from the defined start key.

tricks.original_title: Drag audio directly from the Tracks area into a loaded Quick Sampler
tricks.reason: Rewritten trick, checked independently. Apple confirms the Original/Optimized drop zones and what each does. Apple also confirms that dropping a region triggers an offline bounce, and that the region is bounced through the track's plug-ins. Dragging to the track header opens the 'Replace existing sound' dialog, so the book's capitalization was corrected to Apple's. The closing 'glance over your filter and envelope… rather than assuming everything carried across' has no source either way and was removed. The body was also tightened.
tricks.final_title: Drag audio directly from the Tracks area into a loaded Quick Sampler
tricks.final_body: Drag a region into Quick Sampler's waveform display to swap the sound. Drop it on Original to keep the file's own tuning, loudness, looping and length. Drop it on Optimized and Quick Sampler optimizes tuning, loudness and length, and adds loop and crossfade markers to rhythmic or looped material. The region is bounced offline first. Dragging to the track header instead opens the Replace existing sound dialog.

sources.label: Apple — Add audio to Quick Sampler in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: You can drag a region or audio file into the Quick Sampler waveform display, onto the Original or Optimized portion. Original uses the source file's tuning, loudness, looping and length. Optimized analyzes the file, optimizes tuning, loudness and length, and adds loop and crossfade markers when the content is rhythmic and/or cyclical. Dropping a region triggers a resampling process in which the region is bounced offline. You can also drag to the track header; when the 'Replace existing sound' dialog appears, drag to a Quick Sampler zone.

sources.label: Apple — Drag and drop to create sampler instrument tracks in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The search summary for these Apple results says a region dragged to the track header or another drag zone is bounced through the track's plug-ins. It also describes Quick Sampler (Original) and (Optimized) zones in the 'Replace existing sound' dialog.

tricks.original_title: Use Flex/Follow Tempo to lock a loop to the project
tricks.reason: Rewritten trick, checked independently. The two-button behavior is correct per Apple, but the closing claim that the loop 'tracks tempo changes without shifting pitch' is misleading. Apple says the pitch of the loop still changes with the key you play, and only the speed is synced to the project tempo. That clause was replaced with Apple's wording, and the body was shortened.
tricks.final_title: Use Flex and Follow Tempo to lock a loop to the project
tricks.final_body: Flex and Follow Tempo are separate buttons at the lower right of the waveform display in Classic, One Shot and Slice modes. Flex alone plays the sample at its original speed on every key: the pitch changes, the speed doesn't. Turn on Follow Tempo as well and playback syncs to the project tempo, with slices stretching or contracting to match.

sources.label: Apple — Use Flex in Quick Sampler in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The Flex parameters are at the lower right of the waveform display in Classic, One Shot and Slice modes. With Flex on, the pitch changes as you play across octaves but the playback speed doesn't. After you also click Follow Tempo, the pitch still changes and the playback speed is synchronized with the project tempo. With Flex and Follow Tempo on, individual slices stretch or contract depending on the loop's original tempo and the current project tempo.

tricks.original_title: Set the root key correctly or nothing will be in tune
tricks.reason: Apple's Pitch controls page confirms the Root Key pop-up menu and what it does. The claim 'If your bass is a semitone out across the keyboard, this is why' is an unsupported diagnosis, and 'Quick Sampler guesses the pitch' overstates what Apple documents. The text was rewritten to Apple's description.
tricks.final_title: Set the root key correctly or nothing will be in tune
tricks.final_body: The root key is the note that plays your sample at its original pitch; keys above and below transpose it up or down. If a sample plays out of tune across the keyboard, open the Pitch controls and set the Root Key pop-up menu to the note the sample actually is.

sources.label: Apple — Quick Sampler Pitch controls in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The Root Key pop-up menu lets you choose the keyboard note that plays the sample at its original pitch. Keys below play it at a lower pitch and slower speed; keys above play it higher and faster.

tricks.original_title: Drag MIDI out of Slice mode into the Tracks area
tricks.reason: Apple confirms three points. The generated MIDI region places each slice's note in sequential ascending order, so it plays back as it sounded. The notes can be edited like any MIDI region. Slice mode lets you play the slices in any order.
tricks.final_title: Drag MIDI out of Slice mode into the Tracks area
tricks.final_body: The generated MIDI plays the slices in the original order. Now shuffle the notes and the break rearranges itself.

sources.label: Apple — Quick Sampler Slice mode in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The MIDI notes for each slice are placed sequentially in ascending order, so on playback the project plays the sample as it sounded in Quick Sampler. You can quantize, add or remove notes, and edit them like any MIDI region in the Piano Roll Editor.

sources.label: Apple — Choose a Quick Sampler mode in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Slice mode is ideal for manipulating musical phrases and looped, rhythmic material, letting you play different slices in any order.

tricks.original_title: Convert Quick Sampler to Sampler for full control
tricks.reason: Apple's Quick Sampler overview confirms that content transfers automatically and that the switch is one-way. It does not name 'multiple velocity layers, round robins or key zones' as reasons to switch. What it does say is that you should use Sampler when you need to work with more than one audio file at a time, so the text now uses that.
tricks.final_title: Convert Quick Sampler to Sampler for full control
tricks.final_body: Replace Quick Sampler with Sampler on the instrument channel strip and your current content transfers automatically. Do it when you need to work with more than one audio file at a time. It is a one-way trip: Sampler can load Quick Sampler settings, but Quick Sampler cannot open a Sampler setting.

sources.label: Apple — Quick Sampler overview in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: You can directly replace Quick Sampler with Sampler on an instrument channel strip, and your current content is automatically transferred. Sampler can also load saved Quick Sampler settings, but you cannot open a Sampler setting with Quick Sampler. If you need to work with more than one audio file at a time, use Sampler.

reviews.reason: Apple's Slice mode pages say Slice mode divides the sample into slices based on detected transients, maps those slices to keys, and lets you drag MIDI from the lower part of the waveform display to a software instrument or MIDI track. 'Every hit is mapped to its own key' overstates this, because the number of slice markers depends on the Transient setting and a hit does not always equal a slice. The body is reworded to 'each slice', names the Transient mode the title relies on, and says 'a software instrument track' to match Apple's wording. All URLs were confirmed in search results.
reviews.trimmed_body: Load a drum loop, switch to Slice, choose Transient from the Mode pop-up menu, and each slice is mapped to its own key. Drag from the lower part of the waveform display to a software instrument track in the Tracks area to get the MIDI — the original groove, fully rearrangeable.

verify.search_note: Apple's mixer-view, send, aux, track-stack and colour topics came back only as /10.7/mac/11.0 pages. No versionless page turned up for those. Where a UI name depended on one of those pages, I added an independent source (Sound On Sound, whylogicprorules) or cut the name from the text. Current (versionless) Apple pages confirmed: Show/Hide Mixer = X (Global Commands), Option-click fader = 0 dB (Set channel strip volume), the Solo/Mute gestures (Mute and solo channel strips), VCA send behaviour (Use VCA groups), and Enable Complete Features in Settings > Advanced. The book's "Show Advanced Tools" name is outdated. Budget ran about 3 searches over the target of 12.

tricks.original_title: X toggles the Mixer, and it remembers your scroll position
tricks.reason: No source supports the scroll-position claim, so I removed it. Apple's current Global Commands page confirms Show/Hide Mixer = X. The search result also gives View > Show Mixer and Command-2 (Open Mixer) for a separate window. I dropped the 'faster than the menu' filler.
tricks.final_title: X shows and hides the Mixer
tricks.final_body: Press X (View > Show Mixer) to show and hide the Mixer in the main window, so you can flip between arrangement and mixer with one key. If you want the Mixer in its own window instead, press Command-2 (Window > Open Mixer).

sources.label: Apple - Key commands for Global Commands in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Search result: Show/Hide Mixer is X; Open Mixer is Command-2.

sources.label: Apple - Overview of mixing in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Search result for the mixer topic: choose View > Show Mixer or press X; or choose Window > Open Mixer or press Command-2.

tricks.original_title: Use the Single view to see one channel and its full signal path
tricks.reason: Apple's only indexed page on this is 10.7. Sound On Sound independently confirms the Single/Tracks/All view buttons and says Single shows the selected track's channel strip and its signal flow. I tightened 'every bus it feeds' to the sources' wording, 'signal flow'.
tricks.final_title: Use the Single view to see one channel and its full signal path
tricks.final_body: The Mixer's view buttons switch between Single, Tracks and All. Single shows just the selected track's channel strip and its signal flow: the aux and output strips it feeds. It's the fastest way to debug routing.

sources.label: Apple - Change the Mixer view in Logic Pro (10.7 guide)
sources.evidence: View buttons switch between Single, Tracks and All views; Single shows the signal flow of the channel strip for the focused track.

sources.label: Sound On Sound - Logic Mixer Modes
sources.evidence: Single view limits the Mixer display to a single channel strip, the selected track, and its signal flow.

tricks.original_title: Filter the mixer by channel type
tricks.reason: The filter click and Option-click behaviour is confirmed by Apple (10.7 page) and independently by Sound On Sound, which lists auxes among the filterable categories. The book's closing sentence names 'Show Advanced Tools'. The current Apple setting is 'Enable Complete Features' (Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced), and no current page ties filtering to that option, so I removed the sentence.
tricks.final_title: Filter the mixer by channel type
tricks.final_body: The Mixer's filter buttons limit the display to specific channel strip types. Click a filter button to show or hide that type, or Option-click one to show only that type and hide everything else. When you're setting up sends, Option-click the Aux filter to get a mixer of nothing but your effect returns.

sources.label: Apple - Channel strip types / Change the Mixer view in Logic Pro (10.7 guide)
sources.evidence: Click a filter button to show or hide the channel strip type; Option-click a filter button to show that type while hiding all other types.

sources.label: Sound On Sound - Logic Mixer Modes
sources.evidence: You can filter channel strips by category (audio, instruments, auxes, busses, inputs, outputs, master, MIDI); click a button to enable or disable a type, or Option-click to enable it and disable all others.

tricks.original_title: ⌥‑click any control to reset it to default
tricks.reason: Apple's current 'Set channel strip volume' page confirms Option-clicking the Volume fader returns it to 0 dB. No source I retrieved confirmed Option-clicking a send knob or the 'Reset Channel Strip' menu item, and 'any control' is unsupported, so I narrowed the trick to the fader.
tricks.final_title: ⌥-click a fader to reset it to 0 dB
tricks.final_body: Option-click a channel strip's Volume fader to snap it back to 0 dB. It's the fastest way to undo a level you've talked yourself into.

sources.label: Apple - Set channel strip volume in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Option-click the Volume fader to return it to a neutral level (0 dB gain).

tricks.original_title: ⌥-click Solo for exclusive solo
tricks.reason: Apple's current 'Mute and solo channel strips' page confirms every claim. Option-clicking an unsoloed strip solos it and unsolos the others (Solo Exclusive). Option-clicking an active Solo button clears all solos. Command-clicking a Mute button switches every Mute button in the same state, including the output and master strips (quoted in prior audit, same current URL).
tricks.final_title: ⌥-click Solo for exclusive solo
tricks.final_body: Option-clicking an unsoloed channel strip solos it and unsolos every other channel strip — one gesture to hear one thing. Option-clicking any active Solo button clears all solos at once. Mute has its own bulk gesture, using Command rather than Option: Command-click a Mute button and every Mute button currently in the same state flips with it, including the output and master strips.

sources.label: Apple - Mute and solo channel strips in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Option-clicking an unsoloed channel strip (Solo Exclusive) solos it and unsolos any other; Option-clicking any active Solo button deactivates all solos; Command-click a Mute button and all Mute buttons matching its state switch, including output and master strips.

tricks.original_title: Use VCA faders for level groups without changing routing
tricks.reason: Apple's current VCA page confirms that a VCA changes each member's volume and that post-fader send amounts follow the VCA's volume changes. macprovideo/ask.video add that this keeps the dry/wet balance, unlike an aux subgroup. I tightened the wording and kept only supported claims.
tricks.final_title: Use VCA faders for level groups without changing routing
tricks.final_body: A VCA changes the volume of each channel assigned to it without routing their audio through an aux, so nothing gets re-patched. One consequence: with post-fader sends, what each member sends to an effect follows the VCA, so pulling the VCA down pulls its reverb and delay sends down too, keeping the dry/wet balance. Use Pre Fader sends for anything that must stay constant.

sources.label: Apple - Use VCA groups in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: If you use post-fader send effects, the amount of signal sent to an effect by a channel assigned to a VCA group follows the VCA group volume changes.

sources.label: macProVideo - VCA Groups and Faders in Logic Pro X: What, Why, and How?
sources.evidence: The VCA fader reduces the gain on each channel so post-fader send levels drop too and the dry/wet balance is maintained, unlike sending tracks to an aux and lowering it.

tricks.original_title: Use Summing Stacks for processing groups
tricks.reason: The search confirms Shift-Command-D (or Track > Create Track Stack) opens the Track Stack dialog, where you select Summing Stack. Subtracks' outputs go to a shared aux (the main track). Apple's indexed page for this is 10.7, and Apple's current track stacks overview plus independent results agree.
tricks.final_title: Use Summing Stacks for processing groups
tricks.final_body: Select tracks and hit ⇧⌘D, then choose Summing Stack in the dialog that appears. Everything routes to one aux you can compress and EQ as a unit.

sources.label: Apple - Create and edit Track Stacks in Logic Pro (10.7 guide)
sources.evidence: Select tracks, press Shift-Command-D or choose Track > Create Track Stack; in the Track Stack dialog select Summing Stack, then click OK.

sources.label: Apple - Logic Pro for Mac track stacks overview
sources.evidence: Returned for the same query: a summing stack sends all its tracks' audio outputs to a collective aux track.

tricks.original_title: Create a send and Logic makes the aux for you
tricks.reason: Apple states an aux channel strip is created automatically when you assign a send, except when the bus is already used as an input on another strip. The trick's 'unused bus' wording covers that exception. This is a behaviour claim; the only Apple page indexed is 10.7.
tricks.final_title: Create a send and Logic makes the aux for you
tricks.final_body: Click any Send slot and choose an unused bus. The aux channel appears automatically, already receiving.

sources.label: Apple - Overview of aux channel strips in Logic Pro (10.7 guide)
sources.evidence: An aux channel strip is created automatically when a send assignment is made from a channel strip, except when the chosen bus is already in use as an input source on another channel strip.

tricks.original_title: Set sends to pre‑fader for headphone mixes and effects that must stay constant
tricks.reason: Apple (10.7 page) and whylogicprorules both confirm the three modes: Post Pan, Post Fader and Pre Fader, with the stated volume/pan behaviour. whylogicprorules supports post-fader for reverbs and pre-fader for cue mixes. The 'click the Send knob' gesture came only from the 10.7 page, so I reduced it to the send's pop-up menu.
tricks.final_title: Set sends to pre‑fader for headphone mixes and effects that must stay constant
tricks.final_body: Every send has three signal-flow modes, set from the send's pop-up menu: Post Pan (after fader and pan), Post Fader (follows volume but not pan) and Pre Fader (affected by neither). Use a post mode for reverb, so the effect tracks the part. Use Pre Fader for a headphone cue mix, or any send that must stay put while you ride the fader.

sources.label: Apple - Route audio via send effects in Logic Pro (10.7 guide)
sources.evidence: Send pop-up menu offers Post Pan, Post Fader (affected by volume, not pan) and Pre Fader (affected by neither volume nor pan).

sources.label: Why Logic Pro Rules - Pre-Fader vs Post-Fader vs Post-Pan Explained
sources.evidence: Explains the three send options; post-fader sends typically feed reverbs, pre-fader sends create an independent cue mix.

tricks.original_title: Colour your channels to match your regions
tricks.reason: The body's claim (track colour carries to the Mixer channel strip) is confirmed by Apple's 'Change track colors' page, which the prior audit quoted and my search result echoed. The title says the colour matches your regions, which no source supports, so I retitled it.
tricks.final_title: Colour your tracks and the mixer follows
tricks.final_body: Mixer channels take the track colour. A consistent colour scheme means you find the vocal bus without reading a single label.

sources.label: Apple - Change track colors in Logic Pro (10.7 guide, from prior audit)
sources.evidence: Changing the color of a track also changes the color of the corresponding channel strip in the Mixer (prior-audit quote; this session's search returned the same statement).

tricks.original_title: Bypass with ⌥-click, browse with the slot arrows
tricks.reason: Budget: I did not re-search this. It keeps its prior-audit source, a current (versionless) Apple page that directly documents Option-clicking a plug-in slot to bypass it and clicking the arrows to the right of the slot to choose a plug-in. It was not rewritten.
tricks.final_title: Bypass with ⌥-click, browse with the slot arrows
tricks.final_body: ⌥-click an insert slot to bypass the plugin without opening it. To browse plugins, click the arrows at the right edge of the slot.

sources.label: Apple - Add, remove, move and copy plug-ins in Logic Pro for Mac (from prior audit)
sources.evidence: Option-click the plug-in slot to bypass; place the pointer over the slot and click the arrows that appear to the right to choose a replacement plug-in.

tricks.original_title: Drag plugins between insert slots and between channels
tricks.reason: Budget: I did not re-search this. It relies on its prior-audit source, a current (versionless) Apple page: drag a plug-in within or to another channel strip to move it, and Option-drag to an unused slot to copy. I added 'unused slot' to match Apple.
tricks.final_title: Drag plugins between insert slots and between channels
tricks.final_body: Reorder your chain by dragging a plug-in up or down, or drag it to another channel strip to move it there. Hold ⌥ and drag it to an unused slot to copy rather than move.

sources.label: Apple - Add, remove, move and copy plug-ins in Logic Pro for Mac (from prior audit)
sources.evidence: To move a plug-in: drag it up or down in the channel strip, or to another channel strip. To copy: press and hold Option and drag the plug-in to an unused slot.

reviews.reason: The Single/Tracks/All view names are not supported for Logic 11/12. Apple's only indexed pages for Mixer views are /10.7/ ('Change the Mixer view', 'Mixer interface'), and my Apple-restricted search found no current page. The Sound On Sound article is Logic 9-era: its text refers to 'Mixer Mode tabs', 'Display tabs' and the 'Arrange area'. So neither source is version-appropriate for a UI name. The phrase 'the aux and output strips it feeds' also goes beyond both sources, which say only 'signal flow'.

The filter-button and Option-click behaviour rests on a /10.7/ Apple page plus the same Logic 9-era Sound On Sound article, and neither documents Logic 11/12. An Apple-restricted search for the current Mixer view page found only /10.7/ pages, and those results did not mention Option-click on filter buttons. No current source supports the UI names or the gesture.

Shift-Command-D is supported only by the /10.7/ 'Create and edit Track Stacks' page. An Apple-restricted search of the current key-command pages did not confirm it, and a 10.7 page cannot on its own support a key command for 11/12, so I removed the key. The menu path Track > Create Track Stack was returned by an Apple-restricted search. The current track stacks overview confirms that a summing stack sends all its tracks' outputs to a collective aux track.

Apple says only that post-fader send amounts follow VCA volume changes. Neither source says anything about Pre Fader sends and VCAs, so the closing advice 'Use Pre Fader sends for anything that must stay constant' is an inference about Logic behaviour that no source states. I removed that sentence; the rest is supported by Apple and macProVideo.

tricks.original_title: Compressor — use the side‑chain filter before reaching for a multiband
tricks.reason: The side-chain filter, the HP mode and the kick-drum use case are supported by Apple and by SOS/MusicTech. 'Solves most pumping problems' is an unsupported generalisation, so I replaced it with the documented Listen workflow.
tricks.final_title: Compressor — use the side‑chain filter before reaching for a multiband
tricks.final_body: Turn on the side-chain filter, set it to HP and sweep the frequency up until the kick stops triggering most of the gain reduction. Click Listen to hear what the detector hears. Switch Listen off again before you judge the mix.

sources.label: Apple — Compressor side chain parameters in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Documents the side-chain Filter on/off, Mode (HP etc.), Frequency and Listen controls. The prior audit quote from this page says HP mode can be set so that most of the kick drum's energy is attenuated.

sources.label: Sound On Sound — Logic: Compression Sessions
sources.evidence: Search summary: set Mode to HP and sweep Frequency up until compression on the kick is reduced; use Listen to audition the side chain.

sources.label: MusicTech — Advanced Use Of The Logic Compressor
sources.evidence: Search summary: the Listen button in the side-chain Filter section monitors the side-chain signal path.

tricks.original_title: Multipressor — use it to control one problem band only
tricks.reason: Apple documents up to four bands, each with a Byp (Bypass) button, so leaving one band active is exactly the documented behaviour. 'Dynamic EQ' is an analogy, not a factual claim.
tricks.final_title: Multipressor — use it to control one problem band only
tricks.final_body: Bypass every band except the one you need. It becomes a dynamic EQ rather than a mix‑flattening machine.

sources.label: Apple — Multipressor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Splits the signal into up to four frequency bands, each compressed independently.

sources.label: Apple — Multipressor frequency band controls in Logic Pro for Mac (MY)
sources.evidence: Byp (Bypass) buttons bypass the selected frequency band.

tricks.original_title: Noise Gate — use the side chain to key one sound from another
tricks.reason: Apple's current 'Use Noise Gate' page documents choosing another track or bus as the Side Chain source, which then acts only as a detector/trigger for the gated audio.
tricks.final_title: Noise Gate — use the side chain to key one sound from another
tricks.final_body: Gate a white noise layer from the snare's signal and you have an instant layered snare that follows the performance.

sources.label: Apple — Use Noise Gate in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Pick the triggering signal from the Side Chain pop-up menu. The side chain is used only as a detector/trigger and does not affect the gated audio. The prior audit quote from this page describes gating a strings track keyed from a percussion track.

tricks.original_title: Enveloper — reshape a transient without a compressor
tricks.reason: The two Gain sliders that boost or cut the attack and release phases, and 'add snap to a drum sound', are confirmed by Apple. 'In about four seconds' is unverifiable filler, so I removed it.
tricks.final_title: Enveloper — reshape a transient without a compressor
tricks.final_body: The two Gain sliders either side of the display boost or cut the attack and release phases of any sound. Push Attack up to add snap to a soft kick. Pull it down and percussive sounds fade in more softly.

sources.label: Apple — Enveloper in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The two Gain sliders, one on each side of the central display, govern Attack and Release levels. Boosting the attack can add snap to a drum sound. Attenuating it makes percussive signals fade in more softly.

tricks.original_title: Channel EQ — turn on Analyzer and set it to Post
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Analyzer Pre/Post button: Post shows the frequency curve after EQ is applied.
tricks.final_title: Channel EQ — turn on Analyzer and set it to Post
tricks.final_body: Seeing what you are cutting is worth more than any preset. Post‑EQ analysis shows the result rather than the source.

sources.label: Apple — Channel EQ parameters in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The Analyzer (Pre/Post) button sets whether the frequency curve is shown before or after EQ is applied when Analyzer mode is active.

tricks.original_title: Match EQ — steal a tone rather than guess at it
tricks.reason: This is a rewritten trick. Apple confirms the Apply slider's behaviour (under 100% reduces, over 100% magnifies, negative inverts) and the Smoothing slider. The claim that 'around 40% usually keeps the tonal direction without the artefacts' has no source, so I removed it.
tricks.final_title: Match EQ — steal a tone rather than guess at it
tricks.final_body: Learn a reference, learn your track, and Match EQ builds a filter curve from the difference. The Apply slider sets how hard that curve hits: under 100% reduces it, over 100% exaggerates it, and negative values invert its peaks and troughs. Raise Smoothing to even out a spiky curve.

sources.label: Apple — Match EQ parameters in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Apply slider: values over 100% magnify the effect, under 100% reduce it, and negative values (−1% to −100%) invert peaks and troughs. Smoothing: higher values even out sudden changes in the curve.

sources.label: Apple — Match EQ parameters in Logic Pro for Mac (MY)
sources.evidence: Prior audit quote from this page: Match EQ creates a filter curve based on the differences between the spectrum of the template and the current material.

sources.label: Apple — Use Match EQ in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Apple's how-to page for learning the template and current material in Match EQ.

tricks.original_title: ChromaVerb — use the Damping display as the main control
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the Damping EQ overlay on the main display, which shapes decay by frequency and is edited by dragging dots. 'What makes it sound expensive' is hype, so I rewrote the body using only documented behaviour.

tricks.original_title: Set the Bass Player to follow a specific track's rhythm
tricks.final_title: Set the Bass Player to follow a specific track's rhythm
tricks.final_body: In the Session Player Editor, click Patterns, then choose your guitar or piano track from the Track pop-up menu under Follow Rhythm Of. The bass then follows that part's rhythm, which is how you get a riff-driven arrangement. Apple's own example has the Bass Player following a guitar in the chorus.

sources.evidence: For Bass Player and Keyboard Player, click Patterns and choose a track from the Track pop-up menu under Follow Rhythm Of. Example given: have the Drummer and Bass Player follow a guitar track's rhythm during the chorus.

tricks.original_title: Use the left‑ and right‑hand controls independently
tricks.final_title: Use the left- and right-hand controls independently
tricks.final_body: The left hand has its own Voicing and Style menus; the right hand has its own Voicing and Movement menus. Set the left hand's Style to Sustain Only or Simple and it stays out of the way while the right hand carries the chords, which is useful for comping behind a vocal.
tricks.reason: Separate controls for each hand are confirmed. The original 'keep the right hand busy' implied a right-hand busyness control, which Apple does not document. Movement sets the right hand's note range. The text now names only documented controls.

sources.label: Apple — Edit a Keyboard Player performance in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: You can set voicing types for each hand, the left hand's style, and the right hand's note range with the Movement menu. Sustain Only is a left-hand Style option that plays only long, sustained notes.

sources.label: Apple (MD) — Edit a Keyboard Player performance in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Left-hand Style options: Sustain Only (long sustained notes), Simple (mostly long notes, sometimes short), Moderate, Complex.

tricks.original_title: Set the rhythmic density separately from the complexity
tricks.final_title: Thin out the left hand without touching the right
tricks.final_body: Complexity and Intensity are different controls: Complexity sets how complex the part is, Intensity how loud and intense. Set them with the sliders, then use the left hand's Style menu (Sustain Only, Simple, Moderate, Complex) to make the left hand sparser or busier independently of the right hand.
tricks.reason: There is no separate 'density' control, so the title was wrong. The Style menu's four options and the separate sliders are confirmed. Removed the vague closing line.

tricks.original_title: Convert to MIDI and delete the left hand entirely
tricks.reason: The original body was only an opinion ('fastest route'), and the title leaned on a conversion step it never explained. Rewritten around Apple's documented route: Convert > Convert to MIDI Region gives an ordinary MIDI region you can edit in the Piano Roll.
tricks.final_title: Convert to MIDI, then thin out the part
tricks.final_body: Control-click the Session Player region and choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region. The result behaves like any other MIDI region, so open it in the Piano Roll and delete the left-hand notes to leave a lighter pad or comp.

sources.label: Apple — Convert Session Player regions into MIDI or pattern regions in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region. tricks.original_title: Use Keyboard Player as a writing tool, not a final part
tricks.reason: Mostly workflow advice. The one mechanical step, converting a Session Player region to MIDI, is documented by Apple.
tricks.final_title: Use Keyboard Player as a writing tool, not a final part
tricks.final_body: Generate a progression, convert it to MIDI, then play the good bits yourself. The generated part becomes your reference.

sources.label: Apple — Convert Session Player regions into MIDI or pattern regions in Logic Pro for Mac

tricks.original_title: Try it on a synth patch, not just a piano
tricks.reason: The rewritten text says 'Synth Keyboard Player or Synth Bass Player' as if they were separate players, and says to swap in any pad or pluck. Apple describes Synth Players as Bass Player and Keyboard Player styles. Apple also names the styles and says they load Alchemy but work with any software instrument. Rewritten to those documented facts.
tricks.final_title: Try the Synth Player styles, not just piano
tricks.final_body: Session Players include Synth Player styles. For keys: Rhythmic Chords, Modulated Pad and Simple Pad. For bass: 808 Bass, Pump Bass and Sequenced Bass. They load an Alchemy patch, but you can play them through any software instrument.

sources.label: Apple — Intro to Synth Player styles in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Synth Players are Bass Player and Keyboard Player styles. The Synth Bass styles are 808 Bass, Pump Bass and Sequenced Bass. tricks.original_title: Show the Chord track in Global Tracks
tricks.reason: G is confirmed as Show/Hide Global Tracks. But 'Every Session Player ... will play the progression' is too broad: Apple says a Session Player region follows the Chord track only when it has no region chords of its own, or when its Pitch Source is set to Chord Track. Also added the documented way to turn the Chord track on.
tricks.final_title: Show the Chord track in Global Tracks
tricks.final_body: Press G to show the global tracks, then choose Track > Global Tracks > Configure Global Tracks and select Chord. Session Player regions without their own region chords follow the progression you enter there.

sources.label: Apple — Show and hide global tracks in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Choose Track > Global Tracks > Show Global Tracks, or use the Show/Hide Global Tracks key command (G). You can show individual global tracks, including Chord, via Track > Global Tracks > Configure Global Tracks and its checkboxes.

sources.label: Apple — Choose which chords a Session Player region follows in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: By default a Session Player region with region chords follows them. With no region chords, it follows the chords on the Chord track.

tricks.original_title: Generate chords from an existing MIDI region
tricks.reason: The core claim is confirmed. 'Works on audio via the Chord analysis' was vague; Apple says audio works the same way, by dragging. Added the documented shortcut-menu route.
tricks.final_title: Generate chords from an existing region
tricks.final_body: Drag a MIDI or audio region onto the Chord track and Logic analyses it and adds its chords as a chord group. Or Control-click the region, choose Chords > Analyze Chords, then Chords > Apply Region Chords to Chord Track.

sources.label: Apple — Analyze the chords in audio or MIDI regions in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: When you drag an audio or MIDI region to the Chord track, Logic Pro analyzes it and adds its chords to the Chord track as a chord group. Alternatively, Control-click and choose Chords > Analyze Chords, then Chords > Apply Region Chords to Chord Track.

tricks.original_title: Set chord duration precisely by dragging chord boundaries
tricks.reason: Apple documents resizing by dragging a chord's lower edges. It does not say resizing snaps to the grid: its snap note covers creating chords with Tab, not resizing. The snap claim is removed and Apple's neighbour-resize behaviour added.
tricks.final_title: Resize chords by dragging their lower edges
tricks.final_body: Move the pointer over the lower-left or lower-right edge of a chord until it becomes the Resize pointer, then drag to shorten or lengthen it. The chords either side resize to make room, so check them afterwards.

sources.label: Apple — Move and resize chords in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Move the pointer over the lower-left or lower-right edge of the chord; it becomes a Resize pointer. Drag the edge to shorten or lengthen it. When you resize a chord, the preceding and following chords also resize to fit (prior audit quote from this page; the search also confirms that neighbouring chords resize when you move a chord).

tricks.original_title: Turn Follow Chord Track off for parts that should not move
tricks.reason: The rewritten body is correct: it is Pitch Source in the Region inspector, set per region. But the title still names a 'Follow Chord Track' setting that does not exist. Title fixed, and the Off option Apple documents was added.
tricks.final_title: Use Pitch Source to keep parts off the Chord track
tricks.final_body: There is no Follow Chord Track switch. Select the region and open the Pitch Source pop-up in the Region inspector. Chord Track makes it follow your progression; Region Chords, Key Signature or Off take it off the Chord track. Use that for loops and parts you have already committed.

sources.label: Apple — Control transposition with the Pitch Source parameter in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: In Logic Pro 11 you control how regions and loops transpose with the Pitch Source parameter in the Region inspector. Options include following key signature changes, following the Chord track, following region chords, or Off (does not respond to the key signature or chords).

sources.label: Apple — Choose which chords a Session Player region follows in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: With Pitch Source set to Chord Track in the Region inspector, the Session Player region follows the Chord track; with Region Chords, it follows its region chords.

tricks.reason: Apple confirms the menu path and the M1-or-later requirement. The 11.2 six-stem expansion (adding guitar and piano) is in Apple's guide (prior audit quote) and in two independent 11.2 reports.
tricks.final_title: Split any mixed audio into stems
tricks.final_body: Control-click an audio region and choose Processing > Stem Splitter. Since 11.2 it separates up to six stems — vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and other — and it needs an Apple silicon Mac.

tricks.final_title: Solo each stem and listen before you commit
tricks.final_body: Stem Splitter can leave artefacts: bits of a vocal sometimes land in the wrong stem, and results depend on how busy the mix is and how much reverb and delay it has. Solo each stem from its subtrack header and listen for artefacts before you build on it.

tricks.reason: Apple's newsroom confirms presets for acapella, instrumental and instrumental with vocals. The submix line had the mechanism backwards. tricks.final_title: Make an instrumental with one preset
tricks.final_body: Stem Splitter's presets cover the common jobs in one click: Acapella gives you the vocal, Instrumental removes it. Or tick stems yourself. Selected stems come out individually, and two or more unselected stems are combined into a submix, which you extract by selecting the Submix checkbox.

tricks.final_body: Clicking Apply creates a summing stack below the track holding the selected region, with the extracted stems on its subtracks. The original region is muted so you hear the stems straight away. It is still there if you want to go back to it.

tricks.final_title: Use Drive and Level Out together to stay level‑matched
tricks.final_body: Drive sets how much saturation you get, and Level Out sets the plug-in's output gain. When you push Drive, pull Level Out down so you are comparing at matched loudness. Otherwise you are only hearing louder, not better.

tricks.final_title: Put it on the drum bus before the compressor

tricks.original_title: Check plugin compatibility after updating
tricks.reason: The vague premise was unverified. Apple does document that Logic rescans Audio Units plug-ins the first time it opens after an update. tricks.final_title: Check plug-in compatibility after updating
tricks.final_body: Logic rescans your Audio Units plug-ins the first time it opens after an update. Before relying on a new version for real work, open the Plug-in Manager and look for 'failed validation' in the Compatibility column. Select that plug-in and click Reset & Rescan Selection. If it fails again, check with the developer for an update.
